cards.loText: Explain the impact of collateralization on exposure and assess the risk associated with the remargining period, threshold, and minimum transfer amount.
cards.statement: The margin period of risk includes the grace period allowed to the counterparty before it is deemed to have failed to pay.
cards.explanation: The grace period before a failure to pay becomes a default is one of the time steps; excluding it would understate the margin period of risk.
cards.originalText: Grace period allowed to the counterparty before it is deemed to have failed to pay

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the impact of collateralization on exposure and assess the risk associated with the remargining period, threshold, and minimum transfer amount.
cards.statement: The margin period of risk includes the time needed to settle the collateral that is delivered.
cards.explanation: Settlement time (cash intraday, government bonds about one day, corporate bonds about three days) is one of the time steps of the margin period of risk.
cards.originalText: Settlement of the collateral that is delivered

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Calculate CVA and CVA as a spread with no wrong-way risk, netting, or collateralization.
cards.statement: In the simplified CVA formula with no wrong-way risk, the default probability term is the conditional default probability, i.e. the probability of default in the interval given survival to $t_{j-1}$.
cards.explanation: The default probability in the formula is the marginal (unconditional) probability that default occurs within the interval, measured from today.
cards.originalText: The fourth component is the conditional default probability, i.e. the probability of default in the interval given survival to t(j‑1).
cards.correction: In the simplified CVA formula with no wrong-way risk, the default probability term is the marginal default probability, i.e. the probability of default in the interval as seen from today.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Calculate CVA and CVA as a spread with no wrong-way risk, netting, or collateralization.
cards.statement: In the simplified CVA formula with no wrong-way risk, the loss given default term is one minus the expected recovery rate.
cards.explanation: The first component is LGD, which equals 1 minus the recovery rate.
cards.originalText: The first component is loss given default, i.e. one minus the expected recovery rate.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Calculate CVA and CVA as a spread with no wrong-way risk, netting, or collateralization.
cards.statement: In the simplified CVA formula with no wrong-way risk, the discount factor is the risk-free discount factor for the relevant date.
cards.explanation: Each expected loss is discounted using the risk-free discount factor $DF(t_j)$.
cards.originalText: The second component is the risk‑free discount factor for date t(j).

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Calculate CVA and CVA as a spread with no wrong-way risk, netting, or collateralization.
cards.statement: In the simplified CVA formula with no wrong-way risk, the exposure term is the expected exposure at the relevant future dates.
cards.explanation: With no wrong-way risk, exposure and default are independent, so CVA uses the expected exposure profile EE$(t_j)$.
cards.originalText: The third component is the expected exposure at the relevant future dates.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe debt value adjustment (DVA) and bilateral CVA (BCVA).
cards.statement: Bilateral exposure recognises that when the counterparty defaults the institution is paid only a recovery fraction of its positive exposure, which is a loss, whereas when the institution defaults the counterparty receives only a recovery fraction of the negative exposure, which is a gain for the institution.
cards.explanation: Bilateral counterparty risk assumes that both parties can default: the loss on positive exposure is the CVA side and the gain on negative exposure is the DVA side.
cards.originalText: When the counterparty defaults, the institution is only paid a recovery fraction of their exposure which is a loss for the institution. On the other hand, when the institution defaults, the counterparty receives a recovery fraction of the negative exposure which is a gain for the institution.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe debt value adjustment (DVA) and bilateral CVA (BCVA).
cards.statement: Bilateral exposure is the worst exposure an institution could have at a certain time in the future, measured at a specified level of confidence.
cards.explanation: That describes potential future exposure (PFE), a high-percentile exposure measure. Bilateral exposure refers to both parties being able to default.
cards.originalText: This is the worst exposure an institution could have at a certain time in the future measured at a specified level of confidence.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe debt value adjustment (DVA) and bilateral CVA (BCVA).
cards.statement: If all market participants agree on the BCVA approach and parameters, the total counterparty risk in the market (the sum of all BCVAs) equals the sum of all expected exposures.
cards.explanation: BCVA is symmetric: each party's adjustment is the exact opposite of its counterparty's, so BCVAs net to zero across the market in theory.
cards.originalText: If all market participants agree on the BCVA approach and parameters, the total counterparty risk in the market (the sum of all BCVAs) equals the sum of all expected exposures.
cards.correction: If all market participants agree on the BCVA approach and parameters, the total counterparty risk in the market (the sum of all BCVAs) is zero.

changes.from: equals the sum of all expected exposures

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe debt value adjustment (DVA) and bilateral CVA (BCVA).
cards.statement: The second term of bilateral CVA is the debt value adjustment (DVA), which corresponds to the institution defaulting first, when it books a gain if its mark-to-market is negative.
cards.explanation: DVA is the gain the institution books because on its own default it would pay only a recovery on what it owes.
cards.originalText: The second BCVA term is the debt value adjustment (DVA); it corresponds to the institution defaulting first, when it books a gain if its mark‑to‑market is negative.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe debt value adjustment (DVA) and bilateral CVA (BCVA).
cards.statement: Unlike a unilateral CVA, which can only reduce the value of a position, BCVA can increase it when the DVA term outweighs the CVA term, so the risky value can exceed the risk-free value.
cards.explanation: Unilateral CVA is always a cost, but DVA is a gain that can outweigh CVA, so the bilateral adjustment can be positive.
cards.originalText: Unlike a unilateral CVA, which can only reduce the value of a position, BCVA can increase it when the DVA term outweighs the CVA term, so the risky value can exceed the risk‑free value.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe debt value adjustment (DVA) and bilateral CVA (BCVA).
cards.statement: Netting does not always benefit an institution under BCVA; it can be a disadvantage when the DVA term dominates, which normally corresponds to the institution being riskier than its counterparty.
cards.explanation: With netting, the DVA benefit from negative-MtM trades is partly lost. When DVA dominates, that loss can outweigh the CVA reduction.
cards.originalText: Netting does not always benefit the institution under BCVA; it can be a disadvantage when the DVA term dominates, which normally corresponds to the institution being riskier than its counterparty.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe debt value adjustment (DVA) and bilateral CVA (BCVA).
cards.statement: To value derivatives while reflecting both its own and its counterparties' credit risk, a firm applies debt value adjustment (DVA) together with CVA to obtain bilateral CVA (BCVA).
cards.explanation: BCVA is CVA plus DVA, capturing both the counterparty's default and the firm's own default.
cards.originalText: Implement DVA adjustments to reflect changes in the market’s perception of Acme’s credit risk, applying it in conjunction with CVA to determine BCVA for comprehensive valuation.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe debt value adjustment (DVA) and bilateral CVA (BCVA).
cards.statement: Debt value adjustment (DVA) is no longer a recognised method for adjusting valuations for changes in a firm's own credit risk, so only CVA should be used.
cards.explanation: DVA is recognised: accounting rules since FAS 157 and IFRS 13 require own credit risk to be reflected. Ignoring it reverts to a unilateral CVA.
cards.originalText: Focus only on CVA because DVA is no longer a recognized method for adjusting valuations due to changes in the firm’s own credit risk.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe debt value adjustment (DVA) and bilateral CVA (BCVA).
cards.statement: Debt value adjustment (DVA) has superseded CVA as the industry standard for incorporating credit risk in valuations.
cards.explanation: DVA complements CVA rather than replacing it. Using DVA alone would ignore the counterparty's default.
cards.originalText: Use DVA exclusively for valuation, considering that it has now superseded CVA as the industry standard for incorporating credit risk in valuations.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe debt value adjustment (DVA) and bilateral CVA (BCVA).
cards.statement: Bilateral CVA should be calculated without the DVA term, because including a firm's own credit risk leads to double-counting in the valuation adjustments.
cards.explanation: A BCVA without DVA is just a unilateral CVA. DVA is the mirror-image term for the institution's own default, not double counting.
cards.originalText: Calculate BCVA as an extension of CVA but without including DVA, as including the firm’s own credit risk may lead to double‑counting in the valuation adjustments.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe debt value adjustment (DVA) and bilateral CVA (BCVA).
cards.statement: In Gregory's bilateral CVA formula, the factor $S_{I}(t_{j-1})$ that multiplies the CVA term is the probability that the institution has survived (not defaulted) up to time $t_{j-1}$.
cards.explanation: A counterparty default only hurts the institution if the institution is still alive at that time, so the CVA term is conditioned on the institution's survival.
cards.originalText: The probability that the Institution has survived (not defaulted) up to time $t_{j-1}$

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe debt value adjustment (DVA) and bilateral CVA (BCVA).
cards.statement: In Gregory's bilateral CVA formula, the factor $S_{I}(t_{j-1})$ that multiplies the CVA term is the probability that the counterparty has survived up to time $t_{j-1}$.
cards.explanation: The subscript I denotes the institution. The counterparty's default probability is already in PD$_C$, and its survival probability appears in the DVA term instead.
cards.originalText: The probability that the Counterparty has survived up to time $t_{j-1}$
cards.correction: In Gregory's bilateral CVA formula, the factor $S_{I}(t_{j-1})$ that multiplies the CVA term is the probability that the institution has survived up to time $t_{j-1}$.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe debt value adjustment (DVA) and bilateral CVA (BCVA).
cards.statement: In Gregory's bilateral CVA formula, the factor $S_{I}(t_{j-1})$ that multiplies the CVA term is the probability that the institution has defaulted before time $t_{j-1}$.
cards.explanation: $S_I$ is a survival probability. The probability of having defaulted is $1 - S_I$, and using it would reverse the first-to-default logic.
cards.originalText: The probability that the Institution has defaulted before time $t_{j-1}$
cards.correction: In Gregory's bilateral CVA formula, the factor $S_{I}(t_{j-1})$ that multiplies the CVA term is the probability that the institution has not defaulted before time $t_{j-1}$.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe debt value adjustment (DVA) and bilateral CVA (BCVA).
cards.statement: Debt value adjustment (DVA) is the formalization of a term that incorporates specific wrong-way risk (dependence between exposure and counterparty default) into the CVA framework.
cards.explanation: DVA is the bilateral complement to CVA for the institution's own default. Wrong-way risk is a separate dependence effect.
cards.originalText: DVA is the formalization of a term that incorporates specific wrong‑way risk (i.e., dependence between exposure and counterparty default) in the CVA framework.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe debt value adjustment (DVA) and bilateral CVA (BCVA).
cards.statement: Bilateral CVA is the sum of the credit value adjustment (CVA) and the debt value adjustment (DVA).
cards.explanation: BCVA = CVA + DVA, with CVA a cost and DVA a gain.
cards.originalText: Bilateral CVA is the sum of the credit value adjustment (CVA) and DVA.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe debt value adjustment (DVA) and bilateral CVA (BCVA).
cards.statement: Compared with the risky value that includes only the unilateral CVA term, adding DVA increases the value of the risky position.
cards.explanation: DVA is a gain that offsets part of the CVA cost, so the risky value is higher than under unilateral CVA alone.
cards.originalText: Compared with the risky value that includes only the unilateral CVA term, adding DVA increases the value of the risky position.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe debt value adjustment (DVA) and bilateral CVA (BCVA).
cards.statement: DVA is the mirror image of CVA: it is based on the expected negative exposure, the institution's own default probability and its loss given default.
cards.explanation: DVA mirrors CVA's structure, replacing expected positive exposure and the counterparty's default probability with expected negative exposure and the institution's own default probability.
cards.originalText: DVA is the mirror image of CVA: it is based on the expected negative exposure, the institution’s own default probability and its loss given default.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe debt value adjustment (DVA) and bilateral CVA (BCVA).
cards.statement: If the credit spreads of both counterparties fall while the exposure profiles stay the same, the CVA and DVA recorded by each party are lower in magnitude.
cards.explanation: CVA and DVA are each proportional to a credit spread times an exposure measure. With both spreads lower and exposures unchanged, every adjustment falls.
cards.originalText: Because both spreads fell, the CVA and DVA recorded by each party will be lower in magnitude.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe debt value adjustment (DVA) and bilateral CVA (BCVA).
cards.statement: If the credit spreads of both counterparties fall while the exposure profiles stay the same, the CVA and DVA recorded by each party are higher in magnitude.
cards.explanation: Lower spreads mean lower default probabilities, so the adjustments shrink. Higher adjustments would require spreads to widen.
cards.originalText: Because both spreads fell, the CVA and DVA recorded by each party will be higher in magnitude.
cards.correction: If the credit spreads of both counterparties fall while the exposure profiles stay the same, the CVA and DVA recorded by each party are lower in magnitude.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe debt value adjustment (DVA) and bilateral CVA (BCVA).
cards.statement: All else equal, a widening of a party's own credit spread reduces its DVA.
cards.explanation: DVA rises when the party's own default probability rises, so a wider own spread increases its DVA.
cards.originalText: All else equal, a widening of a party’s own credit spread reduces its DVA.
cards.correction: All else equal, a widening of a party's own credit spread increases its DVA.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe debt value adjustment (DVA) and bilateral CVA (BCVA).
cards.statement: CVA is the cost to a party arising from the possibility that its counterparty defaults.
cards.explanation: CVA is the expected loss from counterparty default and is a cost to the party that is exposed.
cards.originalText: CVA is the cost to a party arising from the possibility that its counterparty defaults.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe debt value adjustment (DVA) and bilateral CVA (BCVA).
cards.statement: DVA is the benefit to a party arising from the possibility that it defaults itself.
cards.explanation: DVA is the mirror image of the counterparty's CVA: the benefit of not paying in full if the party itself defaults.
cards.originalText: DVA is the benefit to a party arising from the possibility that it defaults itself, and (with both parties using the same inputs) equals the counterparty’s CVA on the same position.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the differences between unilateral CVA (UCVA) and BCVA, and between unilateral DVA (UDVA) and BCVA.
cards.statement: Unilateral CVA reflects only the counterparty's default and unilateral DVA only the institution's own default, whereas bilateral CVA reflects both defaults, with each default conditioned on the other party not having defaulted first.
cards.explanation: The unilateral measures each ignore the other party's default. BCVA applies survival (first-to-default) adjustments, so it is not a simple sum of the two unilateral numbers.
cards.originalText: UCVA reflects only the client’s default and UDVA only the bank’s own default; BCVA reflects both, with each default conditioned on the other party not having defaulted first, so its CVA and DVA components are smaller in magnitude than UCVA and UDVA.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the differences between unilateral CVA (UCVA) and BCVA, and between unilateral DVA (UDVA) and BCVA.
cards.statement: Unilateral CVA reflects the default of both parties, while unilateral DVA reflects only the counterparty's default.
cards.explanation: Unilateral CVA captures only the counterparty's default and unilateral DVA only the institution's own default. Bilateral CVA is the measure that reflects both.
cards.originalText: UCVA reflects default of both parties; UDVA reflects only the client’s default; BCVA is exactly UCVA plus UDVA.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the differences between unilateral CVA (UCVA) and BCVA, and between unilateral DVA (UDVA) and BCVA.
cards.statement: Unilateral CVA reflects only the institution's own default, and unilateral DVA reflects only the counterparty's default.
cards.explanation: The roles are reversed: unilateral CVA is the charge for the counterparty's default, and unilateral DVA is the benefit from the institution's own default.
cards.originalText: UCVA reflects only the bank’s own default and UDVA only the client’s default; BCVA reflects both defaults with first‑to‑default survival adjustments.
cards.correction: Unilateral CVA reflects only the counterparty's default, and unilateral DVA reflects only the institution's own default.

changes.from: only the institution's own default, and unilateral DVA reflects only the counterparty's default
changes.to: only the counterparty's default, and unilateral DVA reflects only the institution's own default

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the differences between unilateral CVA (UCVA) and BCVA, and between unilateral DVA (UDVA) and BCVA.
cards.statement: Bilateral CVA can be positive because the debt value adjustment (DVA) may exceed the CVA, whereas unilateral CVA can only be a cost.
cards.explanation: BCVA contains both CVA (a cost) and DVA (a gain). With a much riskier own credit, DVA can dominate and BCVA turns positive, which cannot happen with unilateral CVA alone.
cards.originalText: BCVA can be positive because the debt value adjustment (DVA) may exceed the CVA, whereas UCVA can only be a cost to the bank.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the differences between unilateral CVA (UCVA) and BCVA, and between unilateral DVA (UDVA) and BCVA.
cards.statement: Bilateral CVA is always more negative than unilateral CVA, because it adds the cost of the institution's own default to the cost of the counterparty's default.
cards.explanation: DVA is a gain, not an additional cost, so BCVA is generally less negative than unilateral CVA and may even be positive.
cards.originalText: BCVA is always more negative than UCVA, because it adds the cost of the bank’s own default to the cost of the client’s default.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the differences between unilateral CVA (UCVA) and BCVA, and between unilateral DVA (UDVA) and BCVA.
cards.statement: Unilateral CVA can turn positive when an institution's own credit risk is large, whereas bilateral CVA is always a cost.
cards.explanation: It is the reverse: unilateral CVA can only be a cost, while bilateral CVA can be positive when the DVA term outweighs the CVA term.
cards.originalText: UCVA can turn positive when the bank’s own credit risk is large, whereas BCVA is always a cost to the bank.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the differences between unilateral CVA (UCVA) and BCVA, and between unilateral DVA (UDVA) and BCVA.
cards.statement: Unilateral CVA and bilateral CVA are equal, because the institution's own default cannot affect the value of a trade in which the counterparty is the only party at risk.
cards.explanation: In a bilateral setting both parties can default, and the institution's own default gives rise to DVA, so bilateral CVA differs from unilateral CVA.
cards.originalText: UCVA and BCVA will be equal, because the bank’s own default cannot affect the value of a trade in which the client is the only party at risk.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define and calculate incremental CVA and marginal CVA and explain how to convert CVA into a running spread.
cards.statement: When pricing a new trade under a netting agreement, the CVA charge is the incremental CVA: the CVA of the netting set with the new trade minus the CVA of the netting set without it.
cards.explanation: Netting makes CVA non-additive, so the new trade's cost is the change in netting-set CVA, which captures the offset against existing positions.
cards.originalText: Compute the CVA of the netting set with and without the new trade, and charge the difference (incremental CVA), which reflects the netting benefit.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define and calculate incremental CVA and marginal CVA and explain how to convert CVA into a running spread.
cards.statement: When pricing a new trade under a netting agreement, its stand-alone CVA can simply be added to the existing netting-set CVA, since CVA is additive across trades.
cards.explanation: Stand-alone CVA ignores netting and overstates the charge. With netting, CVA is not additive across trades.
cards.originalText: Compute the new trade’s standalone CVA and add it to the existing netting‑set CVA, since CVA is additive across trades.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define and calculate incremental CVA and marginal CVA and explain how to convert CVA into a running spread.
cards.statement: When pricing a new trade under a netting agreement, the CVA of the existing netting set is sufficient, because the effect of the new trade is captured by the counterparty's credit spread.
cards.explanation: A new trade changes the exposure of the whole netting set. The credit spread reflects the counterparty's default risk, not the trade-level change in exposure.
cards.originalText: Compute the CVA of the existing netting set only, since the new trade’s effect is captured by the counterparty’s credit spread.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define and calculate incremental CVA and marginal CVA and explain how to convert CVA into a running spread.
cards.statement: Incremental CVA is the appropriate measure for charging the desk that has just executed a new trade with the change in netting-set CVA caused by that trade.
cards.explanation: Incremental CVA measures the change in netting-set CVA caused by one specific change (new trade, unwind, restructuring), which is the amount to charge the originating desk or client.
cards.originalText: Charging the desk that has just executed a new trade with the change in netting‑set CVA caused by that trade.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define and calculate incremental CVA and marginal CVA and explain how to convert CVA into a running spread.
cards.statement: Incremental CVA is the measure used to split the netting-set CVA at a given date into trade-level contributions that sum to the total.
cards.explanation: That is marginal CVA, whose contributions add up to the total CVA. Incremental CVAs are tied to the sequence of execution.
cards.originalText: Splitting the netting‑set CVA at a given date into trade‑level contributions that sum to the total, for accounting purposes.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define and calculate incremental CVA and marginal CVA and explain how to convert CVA into a running spread.
cards.statement: Incremental CVA is the most appropriate measure for pricing several trades executed simultaneously with the same counterparty.
cards.explanation: Simultaneous trades are a use case for marginal CVA. Incremental CVA would depend arbitrarily on which of the simultaneous trades is treated as first.
cards.originalText: Pricing several trades executed simultaneously with the counterparty as part of the same deal.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define and calculate incremental CVA and marginal CVA and explain how to convert CVA into a running spread.
cards.statement: Incremental CVA gives each trade's CVA contribution in a way that does not depend on the order in which trades were executed.
cards.explanation: Order-independence is the defining feature of marginal CVA. Incremental CVA is explicitly order-dependent.
cards.originalText: Analysing each trade’s CVA contribution in a way that does not depend on the order in which trades were executed.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define and calculate incremental CVA and marginal CVA and explain how to convert CVA into a running spread.
cards.statement: Marginal CVA is most appropriate for calculating trade-level CVA contributions at a given time.
cards.explanation: Marginal CVA allocates the total netting-set CVA across trades so that the contributions add up to the total.
cards.originalText: Calculating the trade‑level CVA contributions at a given time.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define and calculate incremental CVA and marginal CVA and explain how to convert CVA into a running spread.
cards.statement: Marginal CVA is the most appropriate measure for pricing new transactions.
cards.explanation: New trades are priced with incremental CVA. The marginal CVA of existing trades changes when a trade is added.
cards.originalText: Pricing new transactions.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define and calculate incremental CVA and marginal CVA and explain how to convert CVA into a running spread.
cards.statement: Marginal CVA is the most appropriate measure for pricing trades transacted at different times.
cards.explanation: Trades done at different times are handled sequentially by incremental CVA, which reflects the timing of each trade. Marginal CVA is used for allocation and simultaneous trades.
cards.originalText: Pricing trades transacted at different times.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define and calculate incremental CVA and marginal CVA and explain how to convert CVA into a running spread.
cards.statement: The incremental CVA of a new trade cannot be negative.
cards.explanation: Incremental CVA, through the incremental EPE, can be negative when the new trade sufficiently offsets the existing netting set, so there is no floor at zero.
cards.originalText: It must be greater than or equal to zero; it cannot be negative.
cards.correction: The incremental CVA of a new trade can be negative.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define and calculate incremental CVA and marginal CVA and explain how to convert CVA into a running spread.
cards.statement: Incremental CVA depends on the order in which trades are executed.
cards.explanation: Each trade is measured given the trades already in the netting set, so the order of execution changes its impact.
cards.originalText: It depends on the order in which trades are executed.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define and calculate incremental CVA and marginal CVA and explain how to convert CVA into a running spread.
cards.statement: The incremental CVA of a new trade is less than or equal to its stand-alone CVA.
cards.explanation: Netting can only reduce CVA, so the incremental CVA never exceeds the stand-alone CVA.
cards.originalText: It is less than or equal to the stand‑alone CVA of the new trade.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define and calculate incremental CVA and marginal CVA and explain how to convert CVA into a running spread.
cards.statement: Incremental CVA is useful for measuring the impact of adding a trade to, or removing a trade from, an existing netting set.
cards.explanation: Measuring the impact of new trades, unwinds and restructurings is the primary purpose of incremental CVA.
cards.originalText: It is useful for the impact of adding (or removing) a trade to (from) the existing netting set.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define and calculate incremental CVA and marginal CVA and explain how to convert CVA into a running spread.
cards.statement: By definition, marginal CVA must be less than or equal to incremental CVA.
cards.explanation: Marginal CVA is an order-independent allocation, so it can be above or below a given incremental CVA depending on execution order. No inequality holds by definition.
cards.originalText: By definition, marginal CVA must be less than or equal to incremental CVA.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define and calculate incremental CVA and marginal CVA and explain how to convert CVA into a running spread.
cards.statement: Unlike incremental CVA, marginal CVA is additive: the sum of the marginal CVAs of the trades equals the total CVA.
cards.explanation: Additivity, with contributions summing to the total CVA, is the defining feature of marginal CVA.
cards.originalText: Unlike incremental CVA, marginal CVA is additive: the sum of marginal CVAs is the total CVA.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define and calculate incremental CVA and marginal CVA and explain how to convert CVA into a running spread.
cards.statement: Marginal CVA is more relevant than incremental CVA for apportioning CVA contributions fairly across existing trades or for assessing the CVA of more than one new trade.
cards.explanation: Order-independence makes marginal CVA the fair allocation for existing and simultaneous trades.
cards.originalText: Marginal CVA is more relevant (than incremental CVA) for apportioning CVA contributions fairly across existing trades or assessing the CVA of more than one new trade.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define and calculate incremental CVA and marginal CVA and explain how to convert CVA into a running spread.
cards.statement: Whereas it is difficult to price simultaneous trades with incremental CVA, marginal CVA is the appropriate way to calculate the trade-level CVA contributions of several trades at the same time.
cards.explanation: Simultaneous trades are a stated use of marginal CVA, since it does not depend on which trade is treated as first.
cards.originalText: Whereas it is difficult to price simultaneous trades with incremental CVA, marginal CVA is the appropriate way to calculate the trade‑level CVA contributions of several trades at the same time.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define and calculate incremental CVA and marginal CVA and explain how to convert CVA into a running spread.
cards.statement: Marginal CVA of a trade is lower if the trade is executed second than if it is executed first.
cards.explanation: Marginal CVA is order-independent, so a trade's marginal CVA is the same whichever order the trades are executed in. Only incremental CVA changes with the order.
cards.originalText: W \< V; trade 1 has a lower marginal CVA if executed second than if executed first.
cards.correction: Marginal CVA of a trade is the same whether the trade is executed second or first.

changes.from: is lower if the trade is executed second than if it is executed first
changes.to: is the same whether the trade is executed second or first

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define and calculate incremental CVA and marginal CVA and explain how to convert CVA into a running spread.
cards.statement: The incremental CVA of the first trade executed equals its stand-alone CVA.
cards.explanation: The first trade has nothing in the netting set to net against, so its incremental CVA equals its stand-alone CVA.
cards.originalText: S = 92,593; the incremental CVA of the trade executed first equals its stand‑alone CVA.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define and calculate incremental CVA and marginal CVA and explain how to convert CVA into a running spread.
cards.statement: When trades partly offset each other, a trade's incremental CVA is lower if it is executed after another trade than if it is executed first.
cards.explanation: A later trade gains a netting benefit against the trades already in the netting set, while the first trade has none.
cards.originalText: T \< S; trade 1 has a lower incremental CVA if executed second than if executed first.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define and calculate incremental CVA and marginal CVA and explain how to convert CVA into a running spread.
cards.statement: When trades partly offset each other, the total netted CVA is lower than the sum of the stand-alone CVAs.
cards.explanation: Both allocation methods sum to the same netted total, which is below the stand-alone sum because of the netting benefit.
cards.originalText: X \< 392,973 and Y \< 392,973; total CVA is lower than the sum of stand‑alone CVAs.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define and calculate incremental CVA and marginal CVA and explain how to convert CVA into a running spread.
cards.statement: A risk manager who wants to know which trades have the greatest impact on a counterparty's CVA would use marginal CVA, because it breaks netted CVA into trade-level contributions.
cards.explanation: Marginal CVA uses each trade's marginal expected exposure to split the netting-set CVA into contributions that sum to the total.
cards.originalText: marginal CVA because he could break down netted trades into trade‑level contributions.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define and calculate incremental CVA and marginal CVA and explain how to convert CVA into a running spread.
cards.statement: Incremental CVA breaks down netted CVA into trade-level contributions, so it is the measure to use to see which trades contribute most to a counterparty's CVA.
cards.explanation: The trade-level breakdown is a property of marginal CVA. Incremental CVA measures the change in CVA from adding one specific trade.
cards.originalText: incremental CVA because he could break down netted trades into trade‑level contributions.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define and calculate incremental CVA and marginal CVA and explain how to convert CVA into a running spread.
cards.statement: Marginal CVA measures the change in CVA once a new trade is priced, taking netting into account.
cards.explanation: The change in CVA from adding a new trade describes incremental CVA. Marginal CVA allocates the existing netting-set CVA across trades.
cards.originalText: marginal CVA because it accounts for the change in CVA once the new trade is priced, accounting for netting.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe wrong-way risk and contrast it with right-way risk.
cards.statement: If the correlation between the default of a reference entity and the default of the CDS protection seller increases, the value of the protection to the buyer decreases because of wrong-way risk.
cards.explanation: A higher correlation raises the chance that the protection fails exactly when it is needed, so the expected payoff net of counterparty default, and the value of the protection, falls.
cards.originalText: It decreases, because a default of A becomes more likely to coincide with a default of B (wrong‑way risk), lowering the expected recovery of the protection payment.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe wrong-way risk and contrast it with right-way risk.
cards.statement: If the correlation between the default of a reference entity and the default of the CDS protection seller increases, the value of the protection to the buyer increases because joint default is more likely and the protection is more likely to be needed.
cards.explanation: Joint default means the protection fails when it is needed, so it does not add value. A higher correlation lowers the value of the protection.
cards.originalText: It increases, because a higher chance of joint default means the protection is more likely to be needed.
cards.correction: If the correlation between the default of a reference entity and the default of the CDS protection seller increases, the value of the protection to the buyer decreases because joint default is more likely and the protection is more likely to fail.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe wrong-way risk and contrast it with right-way risk.
cards.statement: The value of CDS protection to the buyer is unaffected by the correlation between the reference entity and the protection seller, because it depends only on the default probability of the reference entity.
cards.explanation: This ignores the counterparty risk on the seller. The dependence between reference entity and seller changes the counterparty-risk-adjusted value of the protection.
cards.originalText: It is unchanged, because the CDS value depends only on the default probability of the reference entity A.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe wrong-way risk and contrast it with right-way risk.
cards.statement: Wrong-way risk is the risk that the exposure to a counterparty is adversely correlated with the credit quality of that counterparty.
cards.explanation: Wrong-way risk is any unfavourable dependence between exposure and counterparty credit quality, which increases overall counterparty risk and CVA.
cards.originalText: Wrong‑way risk

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe wrong-way risk and contrast it with right-way risk.
cards.statement: Concentration risk is the risk that the exposure to a counterparty is adversely correlated with the credit quality of that counterparty.
cards.explanation: Concentration risk is excessive exposure to a single name, sector or region. The adverse dependence between exposure and credit quality is wrong-way risk.
cards.originalText: Concentration risk

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe wrong-way risk and contrast it with right-way risk.
cards.statement: Settlement risk is the risk that the exposure to a counterparty is adversely correlated with the credit quality of that counterparty.
cards.explanation: Settlement risk is the risk that one leg of a transaction is delivered without the other being received. The adverse dependence between exposure and credit quality is wrong-way risk.
cards.originalText: Settlement risk

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe wrong-way risk and contrast it with right-way risk.
cards.statement: Credit migration risk is the risk that the exposure to a counterparty is adversely correlated with the credit quality of that counterparty.
cards.explanation: Credit migration risk is the risk of a change in rating or credit quality, with no link to the size of exposure. The adverse dependence between exposure and credit quality is wrong-way risk.
cards.originalText: Credit migration risk

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe wrong-way risk and contrast it with right-way risk.
cards.statement: One challenge in quantifying wrong-way risk is that historical data is uninformative about it.
cards.explanation: Wrong-way risk may not show up in historical time series or correlations (zero correlation does not imply independence), so history gives an incomplete or misleading picture.
cards.originalText: Uninformative historical data

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify examples of wrong-way risk and examples of right-way risk.
cards.statement: Buying an over-the-counter put option on one bank's stock from another bank creates wrong-way risk, because the performance of the two banks is likely to be correlated and an increase in the value of the put most likely coincides with a deterioration in the seller's credit quality.
cards.explanation: The put gains when the bank stock falls, which is when a correlated seller bank is most likely to be in trouble. Positive dependence between exposure and default probability is wrong-way risk.
cards.originalText: The performance of GigaBank and Alamine Bank is likely to be correlated, and an increase in the value of the put will most likely coincide with a deterioration in the credit quality of Alamine Bank.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify examples of wrong-way risk and examples of right-way risk.
cards.statement: Buying CDS protection on mortgage-backed securities from a monoline insurer whose guarantees are concentrated in the mortgage market is a contract with significant wrong-way risk.
cards.explanation: Protection bought from a seller concentrated in the very risk it insures pays out exactly when the seller is least able to pay.
cards.originalText: Buying CDS protection on mortgage‑backed securities from a monoline insurer whose guarantees are concentrated in the mortgage market.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify examples of wrong-way risk and examples of right-way risk.
cards.statement: Derivatives with a commodity producer that is hedging its output price create wrong-way risk because the producer owes money mainly when prices are high.
cards.explanation: A hedging producer owes money when it is most profitable and least likely to default, so exposure and default probability move in opposite directions. That is right-way risk.
cards.originalText: Derivatives with a commodity producer that is hedging its output price, because the producer owes money mainly when prices are high.
cards.correction: Derivatives with a commodity producer that is hedging its output price create right-way risk because the producer owes money mainly when prices are high.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify examples of wrong-way risk and examples of right-way risk.
cards.statement: Buying an equity call option from a bank on that same bank's own stock creates wrong-way risk.
cards.explanation: A call gains value when the stock rises, when the bank's credit quality is likely improving, so exposure and default probability move in opposite directions. It is the put that carries wrong-way risk.
cards.originalText: Equity call options bought from a bank on that same bank’s stock.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify examples of wrong-way risk and examples of right-way risk.
cards.statement: A derivative with a mining company that hedges its copper price risk typically exhibits right-way risk, because the company owes money mainly when copper prices are high.
cards.explanation: A hedging commodity producer owes money only when it is most profitable, so exposure is high when default risk is low.
cards.originalText: A derivative with a mining company that hedges its copper price risk, so the company owes money mainly when copper prices are high.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify examples of wrong-way risk and examples of right-way risk.
cards.statement: Buying CDS protection from a seller whose credit quality is strongly linked to that of the reference entity typically exhibits right-way risk.
cards.explanation: Strong credit linkage between reference entity and seller produces wrong-way risk, because the protection is least reliable when it is most valuable.
cards.originalText: Buying CDS protection from a seller whose credit quality is strongly linked to that of the reference entity.
cards.correction: Buying CDS protection from a seller whose credit quality is strongly linked to that of the reference entity typically exhibits wrong-way risk.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify examples of wrong-way risk and examples of right-way risk.
cards.statement: Buying an out-of-the-money put on one bank's stock from another bank typically exhibits right-way risk.
cards.explanation: A put on a bank's stock bought from another bank is the textbook wrong-way risk example, since both banks are hit by the same shocks.
cards.originalText: Buying an out‑of‑the‑money put on one bank’s stock from another bank.
cards.correction: Buying an out-of-the-money put on one bank's stock from another bank typically exhibits wrong-way risk.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify examples of wrong-way risk and examples of right-way risk.
cards.statement: An FX forward with a sovereign in which a firm pays the sovereign's local currency and receives dollars typically exhibits right-way risk.
cards.explanation: Paying a sovereign's weak local currency leaves the firm with gains exactly when the sovereign's credit deteriorates, which is wrong-way risk.
cards.originalText: An FX forward with a sovereign counterparty in which Vertex pays the sovereign’s local currency and receives dollars.
cards.correction: An FX forward with a sovereign in which a firm pays the sovereign's local currency and receives dollars typically exhibits wrong-way risk.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify examples of wrong-way risk and examples of right-way risk.
cards.statement: Buying CDS protection carries extreme wrong-way risk if the credit quality of the reference entity is strongly related to that of the protection seller.
cards.explanation: Gains on protection bought from a seller that weakens when the reference entity does may not be collected when needed.
cards.originalText: Credit default swaps where Concord buys protection, which carry extreme WWR if the reference entity’s credit quality is strongly related to that of the protection seller.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify examples of wrong-way risk and examples of right-way risk.
cards.statement: Mortgage derivatives pose wrong-way risk during an economic boom, because a boom increases the likelihood of borrower defaults.
cards.explanation: Mortgage-related wrong-way risk arises in recessions, with falling property prices and higher defaults, not in booms.
cards.originalText: Mortgage derivatives during an economic boom, because a boom increases the likelihood of borrower defaults.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify examples of wrong-way risk and examples of right-way risk.
cards.statement: Financial institutions have countercyclical default probabilities, which reduces wrong-way risk on CDS protection sold on them.
cards.explanation: Defaults of financial institutions cluster in downturns, so their default probabilities are procyclical, not countercyclical.
cards.originalText: Credit default swaps where Concord sells protection on other financial institutions, because financial institutions have countercyclical default probabilities, reducing WWR.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify examples of wrong-way risk and examples of right-way risk.
cards.statement: To limit wrong-way risk on an over-the-counter equity put bought from a dealer bank, the buyer should choose a stock in an unrelated industry whose fortunes have little link to the dealer bank's credit quality.
cards.explanation: Wrong-way risk is reduced by choosing underlyings whose value is not driven by the same factors as the counterparty's creditworthiness.
cards.originalText: Buy a put on the stock of a company in an unrelated industry, whose fortunes have little link to the dealer bank’s credit quality.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify examples of wrong-way risk and examples of right-way risk.
cards.statement: Buying a put on another large bank's stock from a dealer bank limits wrong-way risk.
cards.explanation: Another bank shares the same macro shocks as the dealer bank, so this is the standard example of wrong-way risk.
cards.originalText: Buy a put on the stock of another large bank from the dealer bank.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify examples of wrong-way risk and examples of right-way risk.
cards.statement: Buying a put on a financial-sector index from a dealer bank limits wrong-way risk, since the index diversifies across many banks.
cards.explanation: Diversification across banks does not remove the common financial-sector factor. The index still falls when the dealer weakens.
cards.originalText: Buy a put on a financial‑sector index from the dealer bank, since the index diversifies across many banks.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify examples of wrong-way risk and examples of right-way risk.
cards.statement: Buying a put on the dealer bank's own stock limits wrong-way risk if it is struck in the money rather than out of the money.
cards.explanation: A put on the counterparty's own stock gives the strongest (specific) wrong-way risk, and being in the money does not remove the link.
cards.originalText: Buy a put on the dealer bank’s own stock, struck in the money rather than out of the money.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify examples of wrong-way risk and examples of right-way risk.
cards.statement: A forward currency contract whose mark-to-market gain is positively correlated with the counterparty's default probability is an example of wrong-way risk.
cards.explanation: Wrong-way risk requires a positive exposure to the counterparty that rises as the counterparty's default probability rises.
cards.originalText: Zapex has a position in a forward currency contract where its mark‑to‑market gain is positively correlated with the counterparty’s default probability.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify examples of wrong-way risk and examples of right-way risk.
cards.statement: A firm that has written (sold) a call option to a counterparty in the same industry is exposed to wrong-way risk.
cards.explanation: The seller of an option has an obligation, not an asset, so it has no meaningful credit exposure to the buyer.
cards.originalText: Zapex has written (sold) a call option to a counterparty in the same industry.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify examples of wrong-way risk and examples of right-way risk.
cards.statement: A firm that has written (sold) a credit default swap to a counterparty whose credit quality is positively correlated with the reference entity is exposed to wrong-way risk.
cards.explanation: The seller owes payments under the CDS, so it has no growing claim on the buyer. Wrong-way risk concerns positive exposure to the counterparty.
cards.originalText: Zapex has written (sold) a credit default swap to a counterparty whose credit quality is positively correlated with the reference entity.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify examples of wrong-way risk and examples of right-way risk.
cards.statement: A long oil commodity swap with an oil producer, in which the holder pays a fixed oil price and receives the spot price, is more likely to exhibit right-way risk than wrong-way risk.
cards.explanation: A hedging producer owes money only when oil prices are high, when its business is strong and default is least likely, so exposure and default probability move in opposite directions.
cards.originalText: Acme is long an oil commodity swap with an oil producer: Acme pays a fixed oil price and receives the spot price of oil.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify examples of wrong-way risk and examples of right-way risk.
cards.statement: A long call option exhibits right-way risk if the interaction between exposure and counterparty default probability produces an overall decline in counterparty risk.
cards.explanation: Right-way risk is defined by an overall decline in counterparty risk from the interaction of exposure and default probability.
cards.originalText: A long call option experiences RWR if the interaction between risk exposure and counterparty default probability produces an overall decline in counterparty risk.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify examples of wrong-way risk and examples of right-way risk.
cards.statement: A long put option is subject to wrong-way risk if both exposure and counterparty default probability decrease.
cards.explanation: Wrong-way risk on a long put requires exposure and default probability to rise together, not fall.
cards.originalText: A long put option is subject to WWR if both risk exposure and counterparty default probability decrease.
cards.correction: A long put option is subject to wrong-way risk if both exposure and counterparty default probability increase.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify examples of wrong-way risk and examples of right-way risk.
cards.statement: The 2007-2009 credit crisis is an example of wrong-way risk for a party that had sold credit default swaps as protection against bond issuers' default.
cards.explanation: The buyer of protection held the exposure to the failing monolines. The seller of protection owed the payments, so it was the buyer that faced wrong-way risk.
cards.originalText: The 2007‑2009 credit crisis provides an example of WWR from the perspective of a long who had sold credit default swaps (CDSs) as protection against bond issuers’ default.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify examples of wrong-way risk and examples of right-way risk.
cards.statement: Purchased CDS protection exhibits wrong-way risk merely because it gains value when the reference entity's spread widens, regardless of the protection seller's credit quality.
cards.explanation: Wrong-way risk needs a positive link between the exposure and the counterparty's default probability. A rising CDS value alone is not enough; otherwise every hedge would count as wrong-way risk.
cards.originalText: Both CDS trades show WWR, because any purchased protection gains value when the reference spread widens.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify examples of wrong-way risk and examples of right-way risk.
cards.statement: A purchased CDS shows wrong-way risk when the protection seller's default probability rises in the same scenario that raises the CDS's value, for example when the seller's loan book is concentrated in the same sector as the reference entity.
cards.explanation: Wrong-way risk exists when exposure and counterparty default probability rise together. A seller whose credit quality depends on the same stress that hurts the reference entity has this link, whereas a diversified seller does not.
cards.originalText: The CDS with Seller Y shows WWR, whereas the CDS with Seller X does not.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify examples of wrong-way risk and examples of right-way risk.
cards.statement: Out-of-the-money long put options carry more wrong-way risk than in-the-money long put options.
cards.explanation: An out-of-the-money put has little exposure today and gains value mainly in a severe market fall, which is when the writer is most likely to default. Exposure and default probability are therefore more strongly linked than for an in-the-money put.
cards.originalText: Out‑of‑the‑money put options have more WWR than in‑the‑money put options.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify examples of wrong-way risk and examples of right-way risk.
cards.statement: Out-of-the-money put options have less wrong-way risk than in-the-money put options.
cards.explanation: The relationship is the other way round. An out-of-the-money put pays off mainly in a stress scenario, so its exposure is more tightly tied to the writer's default than an in-the-money put, which already has exposure.
cards.originalText: Out‑of‑the‑money put options have less WWR than in‑the‑money put options.
cards.correction: Out-of-the-money put options have more wrong-way risk than in-the-money put options.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify examples of wrong-way risk and examples of right-way risk.
cards.statement: A long put option is subject to wrong-way risk if both the risk exposure and the counterparty default probability decrease.
cards.explanation: Wrong-way risk arises when exposure rises as the counterparty's default probability rises. Both falling together is not the definition.
cards.originalText: A long put option is subject to WWR if both risk exposure and counterparty default probability decrease.
cards.correction: A long put option is subject to wrong-way risk if both the risk exposure and the counterparty default probability increase.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Discuss the impact of collateral on wrong-way risk.
cards.statement: When exposure can increase suddenly, collateral might not provide significant mitigation against wrong-way risk.
cards.explanation: Collateral only helps if it can be called and received before default. A sudden jump in exposure leaves no time to collect more, especially when the collateral is itself wrong-way, so the benefit is very limited.
cards.originalText: The potential for a sudden increase in exposure means collateral might not provide significant mitigation against WWR.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Discuss the impact of collateral on wrong-way risk.
cards.statement: A rapid increase in exposure enhances the role of collateral in mitigating wrong-way risk.
cards.explanation: A rapid increase in exposure reduces the role of collateral, because extra collateral cannot be called and received in time. Collateral works best when exposure builds gradually.
cards.originalText: A rapid increase in exposure will enhance the role of collateral in mitigating WWR.
cards.correction: A rapid increase in exposure reduces the role of collateral in mitigating wrong-way risk.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Discuss the impact of collateral on wrong-way risk.
cards.statement: Collateral effectively counterbalances any wrong-way risk, regardless of the speed of the exposure increase.
cards.explanation: Collateral is not a universal offset. Its effectiveness depends strongly on timing, and a rapid exposure jump, or collateral that loses value in the same stress, can leave most of the exposure uncovered.
cards.originalText: Collateral will effectively counterbalance any WWR, regardless of the speed of exposure increase.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Discuss the impact of collateral on wrong-way risk.
cards.statement: The effectiveness of margin against wrong-way risk is timing-dependent: only if exposure increases gradually before default can margin be received and offer a mitigation benefit.
cards.explanation: Margin reduces exposure only to the extent it is actually received before default. If exposure builds gradually, margin can be called and received. If exposure jumps near default, the benefit is very limited.
cards.originalText: Margin’s effectiveness is timing‑dependent, and only if the exposure increases gradually prior to default can margin be received and offer a risk mitigation benefit for WWR.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Discuss the impact of collateral on wrong-way risk.
cards.statement: Margin can effectively mitigate wrong-way risk regardless of market conditions, because it is a buffer that absorbs exposure increases irrespective of timing.
cards.explanation: Timing matters. Margin cannot be received instantly, so a sudden jump in exposure between margin calls or just before default is not covered.
cards.originalText: Margin can effectively mitigate WWR regardless of market conditions, as it serves as a buffer that absorbs potential increases in exposure, irrespective of the timing.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Discuss the impact of collateral on wrong-way risk.
cards.statement: When collateral is negatively correlated with the exposure it secures (wrong-way collateral), the dollar volatility of the net position can exceed that of the unhedged exposure.
cards.explanation: Net position volatility depends on the variances of exposure and collateral and on their correlation. With a negative correlation the collateral loses value as the exposure rises, so it adds variance instead of hedging it.
cards.originalText: Scenario C; \$80.0 million collateral with ρ = ‑0.290

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify examples of wrong-way collateral.
cards.statement: Bonds issued by a wholly owned subsidiary of a CDS reference entity are wrong-way collateral, because they are likely to fall sharply in value just as the reference entity's default makes the CDS exposure jump.
cards.explanation: Collateral issued by an entity closely tied to the reference entity loses value exactly when the exposure it secures rises. Because the exposure jumps rather than builds gradually, extra collateral cannot be called in time and little protection remains.
cards.originalText: The DEF Inc. bonds will fall sharply just as the CDS exposure jumps, so the collateral will cover only a small part of the exposure.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify examples of wrong-way collateral.
cards.statement: When a parent company defaults, bonds issued by its wholly owned subsidiary are likely to rise in value as investors move into related debt.
cards.explanation: A parent's default signals distress across the group, so a subsidiary's bonds are likely to fall, not rise. This dependence is what makes such bonds wrong-way collateral.
cards.originalText: The DEF Inc. bonds will rise in value as investors move into related debt, so the collateral will exceed the CDS exposure.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify examples of wrong-way collateral.
cards.statement: A dealer that pays fixed on an interest rate swap and holds government bonds as collateral has wrong-way collateral, because a rise in interest rates increases the swap's value to the dealer while reducing the value of the bonds.
cards.explanation: A pay-fixed swap gains value when rates rise, so the dealer's exposure increases. Government bond prices fall when rates rise, so the collateral loses value at the same time, which is wrong-way collateral.
cards.originalText: It is wrong‑way collateral, because a rise in interest rates increases the swap’s value to the dealer while reducing the value of the government bonds held.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify examples of wrong-way collateral.
cards.statement: A dealer that receives fixed on an interest rate swap and holds government bonds as collateral has wrong-way collateral, because a fall in rates raises the exposure and reduces the bonds' value.
cards.explanation: For a receive-fixed swap a fall in rates raises the swap's value, but it also raises government bond prices. Exposure and collateral value rise together, which is a favourable (right-way) arrangement.
cards.originalText: It would be wrong‑way collateral if the dealer were instead receiving fixed, because a fall in rates would then raise the exposure and reduce the bonds’ value.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify examples of wrong-way collateral.
cards.statement: Government bonds posted as collateral against a pay-fixed interest rate swap are right-way collateral, because their high credit quality means they retain their value in a rate shock.
cards.explanation: Credit quality is not the issue. Bond values and swap exposure both depend on interest rates, and for a pay-fixed swap they move in opposite directions: a rate rise raises the exposure and lowers the collateral value.
cards.originalText: It is right‑way collateral, because government bonds are high quality and so retain their value in a rate shock.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify examples of wrong-way collateral.
cards.statement: When a counterparty posts its own bonds as collateral, the bonds are likely to fall in value as its credit quality deteriorates, so the collateral weakens exactly as its default probability rises.
cards.explanation: Own-issuer bonds are a specific example of wrong-way collateral, because the collateral value is tied directly to the poster's own credit quality.
cards.originalText: The value of the bonds is likely to fall when the counterparty’s credit quality deteriorates, so the collateral weakens exactly as the default probability rises.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify examples of wrong-way collateral.
cards.statement: There is no wrong-way risk when a counterparty posts its own bonds as collateral, provided the bonds are liquid and valued daily at market prices.
cards.explanation: Liquidity and daily valuation do not remove the link. The bonds still lose value as the issuer's credit deteriorates, which is when protection is needed most.
cards.originalText: There is none, because the counterparty’s own bonds are liquid and are valued daily at market prices.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Discuss the impact of wrong-way risk on central counterparties (CCPs).
cards.statement: Higher initial margin at a central counterparty reduces exposure and CVA to a defaulting member but does not eliminate wrong-way risk, because extreme market moves and difficulty auctioning a defaulted portfolio can still produce losses exceeding the margin.
cards.explanation: Initial margin covers potential exposure only up to a finite confidence level. Large, correlated market moves at default, or an illiquid auction of the defaulter's portfolio, can exhaust it and pass losses on to default funds.
cards.originalText: It reduces exposure and the CVA to the defaulter, but does not eliminate WWR, because extreme market moves and difficulty auctioning a defaulted portfolio can still produce losses exceeding the margin.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Discuss the impact of wrong-way risk on central counterparties (CCPs).
cards.statement: Initial margin eliminates a central counterparty's wrong-way risk entirely, because continuous full collateralization removes any possibility of loss to the CCP or its clearing members.
cards.explanation: Margin reduces exposure towards zero but not to zero, since it is set at a high but finite coverage level. Losses beyond margin, as in the Nasdaq default, can reach default fund contributions of non-defaulting members.
cards.originalText: It eliminates WWR entirely, because continuous full collateralization removes any possibility of loss to the CCP or its clearing members.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Discuss the impact of wrong-way risk on central counterparties (CCPs).
cards.statement: A central counterparty should impose higher haircuts on collateral such as bonds issued by the posting member or its affiliates, because their value is likely to fall exactly when the posting member is more likely to default.
cards.explanation: Own-issuer bonds are wrong-way collateral. Higher haircuts discount them more heavily so the loss waterfall remains adequate if the member defaults.
cards.originalText: Impose higher haircuts on such assets, since their value is likely to fall exactly when the posting member is more likely to default.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Discuss the impact of wrong-way risk on central counterparties (CCPs).
cards.statement: A central counterparty should apply lower haircuts to bonds issued by the posting member or its affiliates, since a larger accepted collateral value reduces its exposure to the member.
cards.explanation: Lower haircuts credit the bonds with more value than they will have at default, which worsens the shortfall. Wrong-way collateral calls for higher haircuts.
cards.originalText: Apply lower haircuts to the bonds, since a larger accepted collateral value reduces the exposure to the member.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Discuss the impact of wrong-way risk on central counterparties (CCPs).
cards.statement: Wrong-way risk tends to increase with credit quality, so a central counterparty that sets margin mainly from portfolio market risk implicitly ignores it and should arguably require higher margin and default fund contributions from stronger, more systemic members.
cards.explanation: A large, strong dealer implies more wrong-way risk, but margin based on market risk disassociates credit quality from exposure. Stronger and more systemic members therefore arguably warrant higher margin and default fund contributions.
cards.originalText: She is incorrect, because WWR tends to increase with credit quality, so the CCP implicitly ignores it and should arguably require higher margin and default fund contributions from stronger, more systemic members.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Discuss the impact of wrong-way risk on central counterparties (CCPs).
cards.statement: Wrong-way risk falls as a clearing member's credit quality rises, so central counterparties should require less margin from stronger members.
cards.explanation: The relationship is the opposite: wrong-way risk tends to increase with credit quality, because a default of a strong, systemic member is associated with a large jump in exposure.
cards.originalText: She is incorrect, because WWR falls as the credit quality of a member rises, so CCPs should require less margin from stronger members.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the various wrong-way modeling methods including hazard rate approaches, structural approaches, parametric approaches, and jump approaches.
cards.statement: Wrong-way risk is incorporated into the standard CVA formula by replacing the unconditional expected exposure with the expected exposure conditional on default of the counterparty.
cards.explanation: The standard formula multiplies unconditional expected exposure by default probability, which assumes independence. Using exposure conditional on default captures the dependence while keeping the formula's structure.
cards.originalText: Replace EE(t) with the expected exposure conditional on default of the counterparty.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the various wrong-way modeling methods including hazard rate approaches, structural approaches, parametric approaches, and jump approaches.
cards.statement: The standard CVA expression cannot be adjusted for wrong-way risk and cannot be used when wrong-way risk is present.
cards.explanation: The formula remains usable. It only requires exposure conditional on counterparty default, for example from a hazard rate approach, in place of unconditional expected exposure.
cards.originalText: No adjustment is possible; the expression cannot be used when wrong‑way risk is present.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the various wrong-way modeling methods including hazard rate approaches, structural approaches, parametric approaches, and jump approaches.
cards.statement: Jump approaches account for abrupt changes in exposure, which is critical for capturing the risk of sudden market shifts.
cards.explanation: Jump approaches assume the exposure driver, such as an FX rate, jumps at the counterparty's default, so they capture sudden exposure increases that continuous approaches understate.
cards.originalText: Jump approaches, since they account for abrupt changes in exposure, which is critical for capturing the risk of sudden market shifts.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the various wrong-way modeling methods including hazard rate approaches, structural approaches, parametric approaches, and jump approaches.
cards.statement: Hazard rate approaches are ideal for precise estimation of wrong-way risk, because they offer transparent and easily calibrated correlation parameters.
cards.explanation: Hazard rate (intensity) approaches are easy to implement but generally imply only weak dependence between default and exposure, so they tend to underestimate wrong-way risk.
cards.originalText: Hazard rate approaches, as they offer transparent correlation parameters that are easy to calibrate, making them ideal for precise WWR estimation.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the various wrong-way modeling methods including hazard rate approaches, structural approaches, parametric approaches, and jump approaches.
cards.statement: Jump approaches tend to show collateralization as nearly useless when exposure jumps at default.
cards.explanation: The jump approach models exposure gapping at default, leaving no time for margin to be collected. This matches the observed ineffectiveness of collateral under stress.
cards.originalText: Jump approaches, because they tend to show collateralization as nearly useless when exposure jumps at default.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the various wrong-way modeling methods including hazard rate approaches, structural approaches, parametric approaches, and jump approaches.
cards.statement: Wrong-way risk is not materially affected by how quickly exposure increases relative to margin calls.
cards.explanation: Collateral effectiveness is very timing dependent. If exposure rises faster than margin can be called and received, collateral gives little protection.
cards.originalText: Hudson’s current approach is adequate, because WWR is not materially affected by how quickly exposure increases relative to margin calls.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the various wrong-way modeling methods including hazard rate approaches, structural approaches, parametric approaches, and jump approaches.
cards.statement: The jump approach to wrong-way risk assumes the relevant FX rate jumps by a factor related to a residual value at the counterparty's default time, and the jump is typically larger for highly rated, systemically important sovereigns.
cards.explanation: The jump approach is defined by a discrete move in the exposure driver at default. Evidence shows larger jumps for large firms and highly rated sovereigns because their default is a more significant shock.
cards.originalText: It assumes the relevant FX rate jumps by a factor related to a residual value at the counterparty’s default time; the jump is typically larger for highly rated, systemically important sovereigns.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the various wrong-way modeling methods including hazard rate approaches, structural approaches, parametric approaches, and jump approaches.
cards.statement: The hazard rate approach simulates a stochastic process for credit spreads and computes conditional exposure on paths where default occurs; it is the easiest method but tends to overstate wrong-way risk.
cards.explanation: The hazard rate (intensity) approach is easy to implement but generally shows weak dependence between default and exposure, so it tends to understate wrong-way risk.
cards.originalText: It simulates a stochastic process for credit spreads and computes conditional exposure on paths where default occurs; it is the easiest method but tends to overstate WWR.
cards.correction: The hazard rate approach simulates a stochastic process for credit spreads and computes conditional exposure on paths where default occurs; it is the easiest method but tends to understate wrong-way risk.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe a waterfall structure in a securitization.
cards.statement: A waterfall in a securitization is the set of rules on how cash flows from the collateral are distributed to the various securities in the capital structure.
cards.explanation: The waterfall allocates collateral cash flows, after fees and costs, to the tranches in order of seniority from the top down, with the residual going to equity.
cards.originalText: Rules on how cash flows from the collateral are distributed to the various securities in the capital structure

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe a waterfall structure in a securitization.
cards.statement: A waterfall in a securitization is the process of creating a securitized credit product.
cards.explanation: That describes securitization itself: pooling credit-sensitive assets and issuing new securities backed by them. The waterfall is only one feature of the structure, namely its payment priority rules.
cards.originalText: The process of creating a securitized credit product

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe a waterfall structure in a securitization.
cards.statement: A waterfall in a securitization is a financial intermediary that aggregates the underlying loans and designs the securitization structure.
cards.explanation: An intermediary that pools the loans and designs the deal is the arranger or underwriter (or the special purpose vehicle). The waterfall is the set of payment priority rules.
cards.originalText: A financial intermediary that aggregates underlying loans and designs the securitization structure

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe a waterfall structure in a securitization.
cards.statement: When interest collected on a securitization's collateral falls short of the coupons due, the senior and mezzanine tranches share the shortfall pro rata to their coupons.
cards.explanation: A waterfall is sequential, not pro rata. The senior coupon is paid in full first, so the shortfall falls on the mezzanine tranche and nothing is left for equity or the trust account.
cards.originalText: The senior and mezzanine tranches share the \$0.6 million shortfall pro rata to their coupons, so each is paid slightly less than its promised coupon.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe a waterfall structure in a securitization.
cards.statement: When interest collected on a securitization's collateral is insufficient to pay the senior and mezzanine coupons in full, the equity holders fund the shortfall.
cards.explanation: Equity holders are residual claimants with no obligation to fund shortfalls. When cash is insufficient they simply receive nothing, and the shortfall falls on the most junior bond tranche paid.
cards.originalText: The senior and mezzanine tranches are paid in full, with the \$0.6 million shortfall funded by the equity holders.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Calculate and evaluate one or two iterations of interim cashflows in a three-tiered securitization structure.
cards.statement: In the standard Malz three-tier securitization example, recovered funds from defaulted loans are paid out to the equity holders each year as they are received.
cards.explanation: In the interim years recoveries are deposited into the overcollateralization account together with the diverted excess spread, where they earn interest. Equity receives only the excess spread left after the diversion.
cards.originalText: Recovered funds are paid out to the equity holders each year as they are received.
